content: 1. To evaluate chest pain, first classify the type of angina based on the patient’s description of the pain and findings from the physical examination. Typical angina is characterized by three features: Pain lasting longer than 20 minutes. Pain described as pressure or crushing in quality. Pain provoked by physical or emotional stress and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. If two or three of these criteria are present, it is classified as typical angina. If zero or one criterion is present, it is classified as atypical angina. 2. Calculate the pretest probability of coronary artery disease (CAD) based on the patient’s age, gender, and angina type. Management decisions should then be guided by this probability. 3. Drug side effects include: Nephrotoxicity: Associated with cephalosporins. Ototoxicity: Associated with loop diuretics. Both nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity: Seen with aminoglycosides, vancomycin, loop diuretics, and cisplatin. Pseudomembranous colitis: Caused by ampicillin and clindamycin. 4. DNA is negatively charged due to its phosphate groups. It is composed of nucleotides, which are classified into purines and pyrimidines. Purine synthesis requires glycine, glutamine, aspartate, tetrahydrofolate (folic acid), and CO2. The rate-limiting step is catalyzed by glutamine PRPP amidotransferase. Pyrimidine synthesis involves aspartate, carbamoyl phosphate (providing one carbon and one nitrogen), CO2, glutamine, and ATP. The rate-limiting enzyme is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II. 5. DNA bases include guanine (G), cytosine (C), adenine (A), and thymine (T). G-C pairs form three hydrogen bonds, resulting in higher melting points. A-T pairs form two hydrogen bonds. 6. Histones are basic proteins found in chromatin and are rich in lysine and arginine. Deamination of cytosine results in uracil. 7. Ribosomes are synthesized in the nucleus and transported to the cytoplasm. Eukaryotic ribosomes consist of 60S and 40S subunits, forming an 80S ribosome. Prokaryotic ribosomes consist of 50S and 30S subunits, forming a 70S ribosome. 8. Translation involves: Initiation: Methionine is the start amino acid in eukaryotes, while f-methionine is used in prokaryotes. Initiation factors (IF-1, IF-2, IF-3) assist in assembling the ribosomal subunits. Elongation: Charged aminoacyl-tRNA binds to the A site, and peptidyl transferase transfers the growing polypeptide chain from the P site to the A site. Translocation: The ribosome moves three nucleotides, shifting the tRNA-peptide complex from the A site to the P site. Termination: Stop codons (UGA, UAA, UAG) signal the release of the polypeptide chain. 9. Orotic aciduria is caused by a deficiency of UMP synthase and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. It presents with elevated orotic acid and megaloblastic anemia that does not improve with B12 or folic acid supplementation. Treatment involves uridine supplementation. 10. Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency leads to hyperammonemia and elevated orotic acid due to a defect in the urea cycle. 11. GLUT transporters: GLUT1: Found in red blood cells and the blood-brain barrier; responsible for basal glucose uptake and is insulin-independent. GLUT2: Found in beta pancreatic cells and hepatocytes; regulates glucose levels. GLUT3: Found in neurons and the placenta. GLUT4: Found in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue; insulin-dependent. GLUT5: Responsible for fructose uptake in the gastrointestinal tract. 12. Glycolysis: Hexokinase is present in all cells, has a low Km (high affinity), and a low Vmax. Glucokinase is found in the liver and pancreatic beta cells, has a high Km (low affinity), and a high Vmax. It is induced by insulin. 13. Pyruvate kinase deficiency results in hemolytic anemia due to the inability to maintain Na+/K+ ATPase activity. 14. PFK-1 deficiency leads to elevated fructose-6-phosphate, reduced pyruvate levels, and increased glycogen storage. 15. Regulation of glycolysis: Insulin increases PFK-2 activity, indirectly stimulating PFK-1. Glucagon decreases glycolysis by stimulating fructose bisphosphatase-2 (FBPase-2), which converts fructose-2,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate. 16. Fasting state: Glucagon activates cAMP, which phosphorylates the FBPase-2/PFK-2 complex, activating FBPase-2 and inactivating PFK-2. This increases fructose-6-phosphate and gluconeogenesis. 17. Lead poisoning inhibits delta-ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, leading to basophilic stippling of red blood cells. 18. Atherosclerosis involves endothelial dysfunction, increased vascular permeability, thrombosis, and adhesion of monocytes. Oxidized LDL accumulates, and foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages) form. Smooth muscle cells proliferate, migrate into the intima, and deposit extracellular matrix. 19. Prinzmetal angina is caused by coronary vasospasm and is associated with smoking. It typically occurs at rest, often at night, and is diagnosed via coronary arteriography. Calcium channel blockers are the first-line treatment, with nitrates as a second-line option. 20. Cytochrome P450 inhibitors include ciprofloxacin, ritonavir, amiodarone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, acute alcohol use, macrolides, isoniazid, grapefruit juice, omeprazole, and sulfonamides. 21. Cytochrome P450 inducers include phenytoin, carbamazepine, griseofulvin, barbiturates, rifampin, St. John’s wort, and chronic alcohol use. 22. Disulfiram reaction occurs due to inhibition of acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, leading to increased aldehyde levels. Symptoms include flushing, sweating, nausea, headache, and hypotension. 23. Renin is stimulated by beta-1 receptors in the kidney, reduced sodium in the glomerular filtrate sensed by the macula densa, and low blood pressure sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen (produced by the liver) into angiotensin I, which is converted to angiotensin II by ACE (produced in the lungs and kidneys). Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor and stimulates aldosterone secretion, promoting sodium and water reabsorption. 24. BNP causes vasodilation and increases sodium and water excretion in the urine. 25. Heart valve pathologies: Aortic stenosis: Characterized by an ejection click and a crescendo-decrescendo murmur. Mitral regurgitation: Murmur increases with handgrip and squatting. Mitral valve prolapse: Mid-systolic click with a possible systolic crescendo murmur. Valsalva maneuver causes the murmur to start earlier. Mitral stenosis: Opening snap heard at the apex, often caused by rheumatic heart disease. 26. Aortic regurgitation: Presents with a diastolic murmur immediately after S2, wide pulse pressure, and a water hammer pulse. Causes include a dilated aortic root (e.g., syphilis, Marfan syndrome) or bicuspid aortic valve. 27. Ventricular action potential: Phase 0: Rapid depolarization due to increased sodium permeability. Phase 1: Initial repolarization as sodium channels inactivate and potassium channels open. Phase 2: Plateau phase with calcium influx and potassium efflux, leading to calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and myocyte contraction. Phase 3: Repolarization due to increased potassium efflux and closing of calcium channels. 28. Pacemaker action potential: Phase 0: Depolarization due to voltage-gated calcium channels opening. Phase 3: Repolarization due to increased potassium permeability. Phase 4: Gradual depolarization due to sodium channel conductance. 29. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum synthesizes steroids, lipids, and phospholipids.
